RagShortTexts: Greuthungian leaders depend on followers, households and frontier alliances.
Later Hunnic pressure must not become certain foreknowledge in 374.

Variants.Content: Greuthungian authority on the northern Black Sea frontier draws on rulers, armed followers and relationships among communities. Ammianus's later account of Ermanaric and the Hunnic advance stresses how fear and military pressure can break those connections. That narrative should not become a timetable every character knows in 374. Nor should the module's Greuthungians be equated with the institutions of the later Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy. Internal tension concerns who follows a leader, where dependants can find safety and whether neighbouring groups offer alliance or another threat. Reputation needs practical support when a family is deciding whether to remain or move.

A warrior hears alarming reports from the eastern tracks, but cannot tell which rumour is true. Keeping horses together and finding a defensible crossing matter more than a distant title. If the chief orders movement, the men must also bring children, dependants and supplies; an escape that saves only the fighting party can destroy its support.

A leader needs news from scouts and cooperation from households that may choose another protector. Claiming ancient precedence will not by itself keep allies in place under a new threat. He must consider grazing, routes and the terms of receiving outsiders, without pretending that later defeats or migrations have already settled every choice.
